The distinction is that physics actually gives us several different possibilities:

- **Relativistic time dilation:** Real, measured, and experimentally established. You can effectively travel into other people's future.
- **Closed timelike curves:** Certain mathematical solutions to general relativity permit paths returning to earlier spacetime events. Whether those paths can physically exist is unresolved.
- **Self-consistent histories:** If backward time travel exists, events might have to remain logically consistent. You couldn't change something that already happened.
- **Branching histories:** Changing the past might place you in an alternative history, as *Endgame* proposes. That's speculative, not experimentally established physics.

Inside the sphere, the world had no sound.

Batman could see Tommy running ahead of him, the cracked black sword raised in both hands. He wanted to know which of those worlds was right.

The Grid did not answer.

That, Bruce realized, was the answer.

He had spent his life believing the right preparation could turn a dangerous world into a manageable one. He had mistaken uncertainty for a failure to be corrected. But a world without uncertainty was a world without choice, and a world without choice was precisely what Drakkon wanted to build.

Tommy reached the center first.

"I don't know what the universe cares about."

Drakkon laughed bitterly. "Then you've learned nothing."

Drakkon's face twisted. "Don't pity me."

"I'm not. I'm offering you a choice."

He could have forced the channels into a single path and broken Drakkon forever. The possibility was right there, brutally simple. He felt the shape of it, the seductive certainty of a permanent solution.

But he also felt the people at the far ends of those stolen lines. They were not resources. They were lives. If he closed the path too quickly, the severed connections would tear through the places they belonged.

Bruce opened the band instead.

"Barbara," he said through clenched teeth, "send them home. One at a time."

"You'll be there all night."

"Then we will be here all night."

"Bruce, your suit is burning."

"I know."

At the end only one signal remained: a deep, unstable white-green pulse that belonged to Drakkon himself.

EPILOGUE
Protocol Green

Three weeks later, Bruce Wayne placed a single document in a folder labeled GRID PROTOCOL.

He had written forty-seven pages of observations, seven pages of mathematical approximations, and three separate warnings against trying to treat the Morphin Grid like a conventional power source. The final page contained only five sentences.

The Grid is not a weapon to be owned.

Connection does not confer authority.

Capability does not confer consent.

A contingency plan that removes every choice creates the danger it claims to prevent.

If a Ranger asks for help, begin by listening.

Bruce read the page twice, then closed the file.

Alfred brought coffee to the workbench. "A remarkably short conclusion, considering the amount of equipment you destroyed reaching it."

"The equipment was replaceable."

"So, I am pleased to report, was the roof of Wayne Tower. The structural engineers remain deeply offended."

"They'll recover."

"And Mr. Oliver?"

Bruce looked toward the cave's main platform. Tommy was standing beside the Batmobile, restored armor folded into a compact green device at his belt. The Sword of Darkness had not returned. Tommy seemed less troubled by its absence than Bruce had expected.

"Ready?" Bruce called.

"About as ready as a guy can be to jump between universes."

Tommy climbed the steps to the platform. In the center lay a small ring of carefully arranged sensors. They had not built a Morpher. They had built a window, one that Tommy could open from his side and Bruce could observe without attempting to command it.

The difference had taken them several difficult conversations to agree upon.

"You sure it'll work?" Tommy asked.

"No."

Tommy grinned. "Still learning."

Bruce handed him a small transmitter. "If you need help, this will let you reach me. It won't locate you without permission."

Tommy turned it over. "That's new for you, isn't it?"

"Don't make a thing of it."

Tommy laughed. "Too late."

He hesitated, then offered his hand. Bruce took it.

"You're a good man, Bruce," Tommy said. "Even when you're a royal pain in the ass."

"You talk too much."

"Yeah. But you listened."

The green light opened, gentle this time. Tommy stepped through. Before it closed, he looked back.

"And Bruce?"

"What?"

"You ever figure out how to explain all this to your friends, tell them the truth. You didn't beat Drakkon with a better weapon. You beat him by being willing to need people."

The window closed.

Bruce stood a long time staring at the empty platform.

Alfred watched him from the stairs.

"A rather extraordinary visitor," he said.

"Yes."

"Do you expect to see him again?"

"Probably."

"Shall I purchase more tea?"

"And sandwiches."

"I see our lessons have extended to hospitality."

Bruce returned to the computer. A new message waited on the private terminal.

B: Saw the news. No deaths in the tower incident. Nice work. Also, Dick wants to know if you're still collecting bizarre men with color-coded equipment.

Bruce typed: Tell him I only collect the interesting ones.

B: That counts as a joke. I'm telling everyone.

A second message arrived a moment later, from a number Bruce had not heard from in longer than he liked to admit.

D: Barbara says you asked for help. You feeling okay, old man?

Bruce stared at the words. Then he typed, slowly: Better. Would you like to come by for dinner?

There was a pause long enough for him to imagine every possible rejection. The reply came with characteristic irreverence.

D: Alfred cooking?

Bruce smiled.

Yes.

D: Then I'll be there. Try not to invite any universe-ending warlords before dessert.

Alfred set the coffee beside him.

"Good news, sir?"

"Dick is coming for dinner."

Alfred was quiet for several seconds. "I shall need to order a proper dessert."

Bruce looked at the glass case containing Jason's red helmet. The loss was still there. It always would be. He had learned nothing that could make it smaller. But perhaps there was room beside it for something that wasn't grief.

He switched off the terminal and turned toward the stairs.

"Alfred?"

"Sir?"

"Do you think the Grid would answer if I asked it another question?"

Alfred closed his eyes.

"Master Bruce, if you have learned anything at all from this experience, you will leave the mysteries of the universe alone until after supper."

Bruce considered this.

"After supper," he agreed.

Alfred sighed. It was the sigh of a man who had spent his life raising a child who believed the existence of a locked door was a personal challenge.

Somewhere beneath the manor, a tiny green light blinked once on a disconnected monitor.

Bruce didn't see it.

Alfred did.

He looked at the monitor, picked up the coffee tray, and walked away.

"Absolutely not," he told it.

The light blinked twice.

Alfred kept walking.

THE END

## The story

<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Genre: Action / detective mystery / dysfunctional family drama</text>

**Act I — The family that stopped talking**

Bruce Wayne has built the most sophisticated crime-fighting operation in the world.

Unfortunately, half the people who helped build it no longer want to speak to him.

Dick has established his own life in Blüdhaven. Barbara operates independently in Gotham. Jason comes and goes. Tim is increasingly tired of being the responsible one. Cassandra notices everything, and Stephanie takes tremendous pleasure in irritating everybody.

Damian believes this is all evidence that he's the only qualified heir to the cowl.

Alfred has had enough.

He schedules a family dinner.

Bruce doesn't attend.

There's an emergency.

There's *always* an emergency.

And for the first time, Alfred doesn't accept that explanation.

Meanwhile, a criminal calling himself Hugo Strange has obtained deeply personal information about Batman and the people closest to him. He begins orchestrating public crimes that resemble their worst past experiences, apparently predicting how each family member will respond.

His argument is disturbingly simple: Batman hasn't built a family of heroes. He's built a collection of damaged young people who learned to cope by putting on costumes.

And Strange wants Gotham to see it.

**Act II — The problem with Batman**

The family investigates separately, which is exactly what Strange expects.

He knows Bruce's tactics. He knows Dick's improvisational style. He knows Jason's anger. He knows Barbara's independence.

He has studied every one of them.

The movie's great middle action sequence takes place at an abandoned Gotham rail terminal. Every member of the family arrives pursuing a different lead, and nobody realizes the others are coming.

It becomes a spectacular, completely unnecessary clusterfuck.

Ritchson's Batman comes through a wall.

Nightwing drops from a skylight.

Batgirl has already disabled the surveillance system.

Jason announces himself by crashing a motorcycle through the entrance.

Tim is on the radio yelling that there were four perfectly functional doors.

Damian, naturally, takes credit for everything.

And Alfred, listening from the cave, says:

"How reassuring. An entire family of extraordinarily gifted people, and not a single functioning communication skill between them."

They win the fight.

They lose the case.

Because Strange wanted them together. He wanted their behavior recorded, compared, and modeled.

He has developed a predictive system designed to anticipate Batman's decisions.

And here's the thematic mechanism I want Goddard to explore:

**Strange's model is exceptionally accurate when Bruce acts alone. It fails when the family acts as independent people who trust one another.**

Bruce cannot defeat the problem by becoming more controlling.

That's the very behavior the villain is exploiting.

**Act III — Nobody goes alone**

Barbara identifies the flaw in Strange's operation.

Dick develops the plan.

Jason provides the unpredictable element.

Tim figures out the system's limitations.

Cassandra notices the physical weakness everybody missed.

Damian learns, to his considerable irritation, that sometimes being Robin means listening.

And Bruce?

Bruce has to trust them.

Not because he has exhausted every other option.

Because he recognizes their judgment.

The climax is still spectacular. Ritchson gets his massive Batman fight, hammering through Strange's hired muscle in a collapsing Gotham railway station.

But when Strange attempts to escape, Bruce has a choice: pursue him alone or help the rest of the family get civilians out safely.

This Batman chooses his family.

Barbara catches Strange.

And she is absolutely delighted to inform Bruce that she did not require his permission.

# BATMAN: FAMILY BUSINESS

*A Bat-Family Novel*

*An unofficial work of fan fiction, imagined with Alan Ritchson as Bruce Wayne in an alternate DC Universe.*

## Dramatis Personae

**Bruce Wayne / Batman** — Alan Ritchson  
**Dick Grayson / Nightwing** — Tanner Buchanan  
**Barbara Gordon / Batgirl** — Leslie Grace  
**Jason Todd / Red Hood** — D'Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai  
**Tim Drake / Red Robin** — Jaeden Martell  
**Cassandra Cain / Orphan** — Miya Cech  
**Stephanie Brown / Spoiler** — Mckenna Grace  
**Damian Wayne / Robin** — Gordon Cormier  
**Alfred Pennyworth** — Hugh Laurie  
**Commissioner James Gordon** — J.K. Simmons  
**Lucius Fox** — Colman Domingo  
**Dr. Hugo Strange** — Walton Goggins  
**Arnold Wesker / the Ventriloquist** — Paul Walter Hauser  
**Scarface (voice)** — Alan Tudyk

*An imagined production: story oversight by James Gunn; screenplay sensibility by Drew Goddard; directed, in the author's dream world, by Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah. This novel is original prose, not an adaptation of an existing film.*

# Prologue — A Reliable Prediction

The first thing Hugo Strange told the deputy mayor was that Gotham had become frighteningly easy to understand.

The deputy mayor was not pleased to hear it. He had arrived expecting a funding request and possibly lunch. Instead he found himself in a windowless demonstration room beneath a municipal annex, facing a wall of screens that displayed his city in tiny moving squares.

Traffic. Ambulance dispatches. Weather alerts. Transit interruptions. A woman crossing an avenue with a dog. A truck double-parked outside a bakery. All the ordinary, unimportant things that became important the moment they went wrong.

"We don't know where Batman is," Deputy Mayor Pike said.

"Of course not." Strange smiled. The effect was comfortable until one noticed that his eyes had not participated. "That would be a rather poor magic trick if we did. But we can know where he is going."

He touched a key on the table. Three cameras enlarged an intersection in the Narrows, where a contractor's van had apparently struck a fire hydrant. Water hissed into the road. A city bus stopped at an angle to the curb. A boy in a school uniform watched it from the sidewalk.

"Seven minutes ago," Strange said, "our model predicted that an accident at this intersection would attract first responders, that the westbound bus would be delayed, and that Batman would choose the roofs to the south rather than the elevated railway to the north."

"A model," Pike repeated.

"A tool. I wouldn't ask it to choose a wife, for instance. Although I suspect it would do tolerably well at predicting a divorce."

A shadow crossed one of the rooftops. Pike leaned toward the screen as if that could make the image clearer. A broad-shouldered figure appeared beneath a billboard, black cape moving against the wet brick.

"There," Strange said softly.

Batman vanished between buildings. The cursor on the demonstration screen moved to another square. Two seconds later, Batman appeared there.

Pike stared. "Christ."

"A word often used when someone mistakes preparation for omniscience."

The deputy mayor had heard rumors about the Gotham Continuity Initiative, an expensive plan to coordinate emergency services when the city's aging systems failed. The interface in front of him certainly looked expensive. That did not explain why a psychiatrist was running it.

"You're supposed to be advising on trauma response," Pike said.

"I am. What is Gotham if not an extended trauma response?"

At the back of the room, behind smoked glass, a small man waited on a folding chair with a wooden puppet across his knees. The puppet wore a pinstriped suit and a hat pulled over one painted eye. Its little shoes were shined. The man beside it kept smoothing the lapels as though afraid the fabric might suffer embarrassment.

The puppet turned toward the room.

"Ya gonna tell 'im the part where ya need my boys, Doc?"

Pike flinched. Strange did not.

"Mr. Wesker has agreed to assist with a limited field test," he said.

"I didn't agree to—" The little man stopped, caught by the puppet's sudden movement. His face changed. "Course we did. We like tests. Long as we get paid."

"Who is that?" Pike whispered.

"A consultant."

"That is a *puppet*."

"Then I should very much like to see what it says about your hiring practices."

On the wall, a fourth window opened. It showed Bruce Wayne shaking hands with donors at a hospital gala. Beside him stood a younger man whose smile did not reach his eyes. In another photograph a woman in a motorcycle jacket was arguing with Bruce on the steps of Wayne Tower. Then a boy with dark hair. Another young man. A young woman with her hands tucked into a coat. Faces rearranged themselves around Wayne in a loose constellation.

Pike looked away. "What have they got to do with it?"

Strange watched the photographs with a physician's delighted attention to a surprising symptom.

"A great deal," he said.

He enlarged the photograph of the man beside Bruce Wayne. Beneath it, a line of machine-generated text read: **PERMISSION TO ACT: HISTORICALLY DENIED**.

"You cannot predict a city," Strange said, "until you understand what its most powerful man is afraid to lose."

A green line appeared on the map, joining twelve cameras from one end of Gotham to the other. It looked almost like a stitch closing a wound.

"Tomorrow," Strange told Pike, "we shall discover what Batman does when there is more than one person to save."

The puppet laughed. The man holding it looked sick.

# Chapter One — An Invitation Is Not a Summons

Alfred Pennyworth had set a place for Richard Grayson three times in the last eighteen months.

On each occasion the young man had canceled. Once because of a fire in Blüdhaven. Once because he was on another continent. The third time he had simply said he couldn't. Alfred, who had known Dick since he was a frightened child with circus-callused palms, had recognized the distinction between unable and unwilling.

This Saturday, however, Richard had said yes.

That made the kitchen unusually dangerous.

"You have sixteen kilograms of potatoes," Bruce Wayne observed from the doorway.

Alfred did not look up from the chopping board. "You are welcome to count them again, sir. It might prevent you from interfering with the actual cooking."

Bruce had showered but not slept. A bruise crossed his ribs beneath the gray shirt. There was a deep scratch at his temple and another across the base of his thumb. His six-foot-four frame made the doorway appear as if the builders had miscalculated an average man's size by a considerable margin.

"Nine people don't need sixteen kilograms."

"Nine people include Master Jason."

"Jason isn't coming."

"Master Jason has informed me, in language so colorful that even the gardeners expressed professional curiosity, that he will be arriving precisely on time."

Bruce considered this.

"Why?"

"Food, I believe. A concept with which your relationship remains regrettably theoretical."

A small package rested on the kitchen counter beside the potatoes. Bruce recognized it: a hand-built transmitter, no bigger than an old pager, with a green mark on its side. His recent guest had left a second one behind. Tommy Oliver had traveled home three weeks earlier, after a disagreement involving a stolen power source, a man wearing white-and-green armor, and the near destruction of Wayne Tower. Tommy had left Bruce with an unusual problem.

He had demonstrated that asking for help did not necessarily lead to catastrophe.

The lesson had proved harder to retain than the damage reports.

"Are you inviting the entire team?" Bruce asked.

"The family, sir. And they have names."

"They have operational responsibilities."

Alfred laid down the knife. "Do you intend to put them on the menu?"

Bruce folded his arms, a movement that made his ribs complain.

"I'm asking about security."

"You are asking whether your own household is safe for the people who used to live in it. I should find the distinction humiliating, were I not so practiced at forgiving you."

There were times when Bruce wished Alfred would simply shout. The gentleness made it almost impossible to argue.

"Dick said he's coming," Bruce said.

"Yes. Barbara, too. Commissioner Gordon is occupied with an equally exhausting family affair involving an actual police department, but hopes to arrive for coffee."

"Barbara hasn't answered my last six messages."

"She answered mine on the first ring."

Bruce looked toward the clock. "There's still a chance I may be late."

"There always is, sir."

From the window, Gotham stood beyond the estate like a collection of unfinished arguments. In daylight the city almost looked ordinary. At night it glowed like an electrical fault.

"If anything happens—"

"You have seven extraordinarily capable colleagues, a police commissioner who remembers how to use a telephone, and a young man named Tim who has built an alarm system so irritatingly redundant that it informed me of an armed robbery at a shop in Lisbon. If something happens, they can manage it for the duration of one dinner."

Bruce had no response prepared for that.

Alfred returned to the potatoes. "There is one further requirement."

"What?"

"No surveillance at the table."

Bruce was quiet for long enough that Alfred finally looked up.

"Master Bruce."

"It's turned off."

"I didn't ask whether the equipment is turned off. I asked you not to turn your guests into an operation."

Bruce looked down at his scarred hand. He had once been very good at making promises in the shape of orders. A strange green visitor had recently informed him that they were not the same thing.

"All right," he said.

Alfred gave a small nod. "Very good. Now please go and find something to wear that does not imply you plan to interrogate your dinner."

"It's a gray shirt."

"Precisely."

Bruce went upstairs. The transmitter blinked once on the counter.

Alfred regarded it.

"Not today," he told the small green light.

It stopped.

Alfred decided not to mention that to anyone.

# Chapter Two — Three Rings

Dick Grayson counted the rings because he knew the voice on the other end was counting them too.

One.

Two.

Three.

"You know," Barbara Gordon said when she answered, "if you wanted to avoid this, you could have called Alfred and invented a fire."

"Used it. Eighteen months ago."

"Right. The unconvincing fire."

Dick stood beside a coffee shop window in Blüdhaven, wearing a jacket that probably cost more than his first apartment and sneakers that definitely did not. He watched a little girl outside argue with her father about whether pigeons understood insults.

"You going?" he asked.

"Yes."

"Really?"

"Alfred asked. It's his roast. I'm not punishing the roast for Bruce's decisions."

"A noble distinction."

"I contain multitudes."

Dick rolled his shoulders. A bruise from last night's patrol made itself known. He could have rehearsed the things he planned to say to Bruce, but he had been doing that for years and the words never sounded the same aloud.

The trouble was that there hadn't been one fight. There had been dozens, separated by stretches of normalcy so convincing that Dick had stopped noticing how angry he was. Bruce could be generous with money, dangerous with secrets, and astonishingly miserly with apologies. He loved people as if love were an emergency procedure with instructions only he could read.

"He asked me," Dick said.

Barbara went quiet. "What?"

"He actually asked. Not 'report to the cave.' Not 'need you in Gotham.' He sent a message saying, 'Would you like to come by for dinner?' And then he waited."

"Did he sign it?"

"No."

"We should probably rule out a body-snatcher."

"Alfred says a guy in green armor taught him manners."

"Tommy Oliver. I spoke to him."

Dick stopped walking. "You met the mysterious armored visitor and didn't tell me?"

"I monitored him from a safe distance while Bruce tried to understand an impossible energy source. The visitor told him to ask permission. Bruce looked like someone had offered to remove his spine."

"I would've paid actual money to see that."

"I have footage."

"Barbara."

"Kidding. Mostly."

They laughed. For a minute it was easy; it felt like being seventeen and working out how to sneak a motorcycle into the cave without waking Alfred.

Then Barbara said, "I'm not coming to help him pretend nothing happened."

Dick looked at the pigeons. The little girl had won. Her father was now apologizing to a bird.

"Neither am I."

"Good."

"But I think I'm done rehearsing what I want him to say."

"That's healthy. Disturbing, but healthy."

The call ended. Dick took a second to look at the photograph on his phone: himself and Bruce outside a circus tent, both younger, smiling. The photo had been taken on a good day. There were more good days than his anger sometimes allowed him to remember.

He put the phone away and headed toward Gotham.

* * *

Barbara Gordon had three rules for walking into Wayne Manor. She would not bring her costume. She would not talk about casework over dinner. And if Bruce tried to tell her what to do, she would leave before the salad.

She repeated the rules while fitting a wireless monitor into a compact black case, then reconsidered the third one. Leaving before the salad punished Alfred. She could at least finish the first course.

A news feed crawled across a separate screen. Gotham's city council had approved a pilot program called the Continuity Initiative, intended to coordinate emergency response data during infrastructure failures. The vendor, a little-known analytics company named Bellwether Civic, had received permission to use anonymized historical incident records.

Barbara highlighted the phrase *anonymized* and made a face.

The consent agreement appeared to have been drafted by somebody who confused hiding a name with protecting a person.

Her father called as she was shutting down the display.

"Dinner tonight?" Gordon asked.

"Wayne Manor. Alfred invited me."

"Ah."

"That 'ah' is doing a lot of work."

"I'm your father. I'm permitted a small amount of editorial expression."

"You can come for coffee."

"I have a missing person case and a mayor who keeps leaving his own security detail. But I'll try."

Barbara slipped her jacket on. "You sound tired."

"You sound like your mother."

"She was right a remarkable percentage of the time."

"Yes," Gordon said softly. "She was."

The case on the monitor flashed once more before Barbara closed it. A vehicle collision in the Narrows, categorized as a routine event, had been flagged by Bellwether as *test successful*. The annotation had appeared in a public logging channel for twelve seconds, then vanished.

Barbara stared at the blank screen.

She had promised herself not to work tonight.

She took a photograph of the log anyway.

# Chapter Three — A Normal Dinner, More or Less

Alfred had bought flowers.

This alone was enough to make Dick suspicious.

The front hall of Wayne Manor smelled of polished wood, roasting garlic, and a home that had survived too many seasons by refusing to admit it was lonely. Dick remembered running along these corridors as a boy, Alfred calling after him not to slide down the banister, Bruce pretending not to notice when he did. He remembered Jason laughing in the library before anyone understood how little time they would have together.

He remembered leaving.

"Master Richard," Alfred said.

Dick tried to answer and discovered he had an armful of elderly Englishman instead. They hugged, tightly and without any of the caution that Wayne Manor usually inspired.

"Good to see you," Dick said into Alfred's shoulder.

"An opinion I share with unusual intensity. You are early."

"I'm capable of personal growth."

"I shall inform the newspapers."

Someone cleared her throat behind him. Barbara stood in the open doorway, one eyebrow raised, carrying a bottle of wine and the sort of expression that suggested she had already identified twelve possible exits.

"You're blocking the entrance," she said.

"I'm the favorite. I get priority hugs."

"You are the loudest. It is not the same distinction."

Alfred hugged her too.

Within twenty minutes the house had filled with noise it had spent years missing. Tim arrived carrying a case of board games and immediately confessed he had not read any rules. Stephanie was beside him, delighted. Cassandra came next with a small bunch of pale flowers she had picked from the manor's outer walk because she thought the expensive ones looked unhappy. Alfred thanked her as though she had brought him the crown jewels.

Damian appeared from an upstairs corridor wearing a tailored jacket and an expression of strained tolerance.

"I was informed this would be a civilized event," he announced.

"It is," Dick said. "That's why nobody invited your attitude."

"Your jokes remain derivative, Grayson."

"And yet you keep laughing at them."

"I have never laughed at one of your jokes."

Cassandra tapped Damian's sleeve, then gently raised the corners of his mouth with two fingers.

Stephanie nearly dropped her glass.

Jason arrived last, exactly on time. He stepped inside wearing a leather jacket with a broken zipper and carrying an enormous bakery box.

"What's that?" Tim asked.

"Emergency dessert."

"Alfred made dessert."

"That's why it's an emergency."

Alfred examined the box, saw the chocolate cake, and wisely accepted it as a compliment.

Seven people sat at the table before Bruce arrived. That was the first problem.

"He'll be here," Alfred told them.

Nobody asked where Bruce was. They all knew the silence that followed his absence; it had been part of this household as surely as the portraits.

At eight forty-seven, the dining-room door opened.

Bruce stood in the doorway with his tie loosened, his hair still damp, and blood showing beneath the cuff of his shirt.

"Sorry I'm late."

Jason looked at the blood. "Did the valet shoot you?"

"No."

"Disappointing. I had a whole speech prepared about tipping."

Bruce took in the table: Dick beside Barbara, Tim with Stephanie, Cassandra leaning comfortably between Alfred and Damian, Jason with the cake, the lights warm against the old carved wood. For a moment he looked as though he had encountered an impossible technology.

"You came," he said to Dick.

Dick nodded. "Alfred cooked."

"He told me."

"That's a sentence I'm still getting used to."

Bruce sat. Alfred brought another plate and made no comment about the blood, which in this family was the surest signal that an argument had merely been postponed.

Dinner began tentatively. Jason described a local street racer who had attempted to outrun his motorcycle using a rented electric scooter. Stephanie accused Tim of creating an hourly alert for Gotham's restaurant inspection scores. Tim denied it, then admitted he had once examined the data for patterns in municipal corruption. Cassandra silently stole one of Damian's rolls. Damian informed her that theft was undignified, then offered her the butter.

Bruce listened. It was not an activity at which he had much practice.

"You look different," Barbara said at last.

Bruce looked up. "I am different."

"Different how?"

"I'm attempting to have dinner without asking where everyone was last night."

"You mean you've reached adulthood," Jason said.

"Jason," Alfred warned.

"What? I said *attempting*."

Dick nearly smiled. Then Bruce said, "I heard about the Blüdhaven docks."

The table changed temperature.

"Of course you did," Dick said.

Bruce felt it immediately and tried to stop. "I wasn't going to—"

"You weren't going to what? Ask why I didn't call? Tell me you could've handled it better? Send a list of people I should interrogate?"

"I was going to say you did good work."

Dick blinked. Barbara studied Bruce with renewed interest.

"Oh," Dick said.

"You did."

"Thank you."

Something fragile settled in the space between them. Bruce could almost hear the air moving around it.

Then every phone at the table sounded the same warning.

Not a ringtone. A single low note followed by a municipal emergency tone.

Tim checked his screen first. "That's not right."

Alfred's kitchen display lit up. The television in the neighboring sitting room switched itself on. A projection appeared on the dining-room wall, assembled from a dozen photographs taken over the years: Bruce beside Dick, Barbara on a motorcycle, Jason with a split lip, Tim in front of a computer, the younger faces threaded between them.

A warm voice spoke.

"Good evening, Mr. Wayne. I trust the meal has been pleasant."

Bruce stood so quickly his chair scraped the floor.

"Who is that?" Stephanie asked.

Barbara recognized the voice from a psychiatric conference recording. "Hugo Strange."

On the wall, a diagram appeared: circles joined to other circles with thin lines. Each circle carried a name. In the center was a silhouette unmistakably shaped like Batman.

**PREDICTED RESPONSE HIERARCHY: CENTRAL AUTHORITY — BRUCE WAYNE.**

"An interesting family," Strange continued. "So many talented people. And yet one finds the same problem in every arrangement. Nobody appears permitted to make a mistake unless the head of the household has first approved it."

"Turn it off," Bruce said.

Barbara drew her phone from her pocket. "Don't touch anything."

Bruce reached for the wall panel.

"Bruce," she said sharply.

He stopped.

The voice continued. "This isn't a threat. Not yet. It's an invitation. Tomorrow evening, the city will watch the family work. I believe your neighbors deserve to know what kind of protection they have purchased."

The image vanished. The lights returned to normal. Somewhere in the hall a grandfather clock struck nine.

Bruce looked around the table. Everyone was staring at him.

He opened his mouth, intending to say *we need to go to the cave*, and saw Dick's expression change in anticipation of the order.

Bruce closed his mouth.

"What do you think?" he asked Barbara.

Nobody moved.

"I think," Barbara said carefully, "that somebody has spent a long time studying us."

"And?"

"And I think the first thing we should do is find out what he knows without automatically giving him more."

"Good," Bruce said.

Jason leaned back. "Jesus Christ. Who taught him to ask questions?"

"A friend," Bruce said.

Alfred picked up his wineglass. It was an unexpectedly promising beginning to an extraordinarily bad evening.

They had erected banks with Roman columns, courthouses with marble steps, and monuments to virtues they rarely practiced. The room went cold. Arnold's fingers tightened inside the puppet's back. Scarface tilted his chin.

"Watch your mouth, Doc."

Strange crouched so that his face was level with the puppet's.

Scarface leaned forward.

Arnold felt the wooden jaw move beneath his thumb.

"That sounds," he whispered, "like a terrible thing to do to a family."

Strange's smile did not change.

CHAPTER ONE
Nine Places

Alfred Pennyworth had survived a war, several attempts on his life, two generations of Wayne family secrets, and the arrival of a boy who had once concealed a throwing knife in the Christmas pudding.

He considered none of these experiences adequate preparation for arranging a family dinner.

The problem was not the food. The food was excellent. The problem was the nine places Alfred had set around the long table in Wayne Manor's smaller dining room.

Bruce was at one end, nominally. Alfred sat at the other, against all the instincts of a man who had spent most of his life standing while other people ate. Between them, he had arranged places for Dick, Barbara, Jason, Tim, Cassandra, Stephanie, and Damian.

There were eight people in the house. Bruce was not one of them.

At seven twenty, Dick Grayson arrived carrying a bottle of wine and the guarded expression of a man entering a room where he had once been happy.

"You're early," Alfred said.

"Traffic wasn't terrible. I assume the apocalypse is scheduled for nine."

Alfred took the bottle. "That would allow us time for the cheese course."

Dick hugged him. It was quick, fierce, and almost enough to make Alfred forget the empty chair waiting upstairs.

Barbara Gordon entered two minutes later, dressed in black trousers and a jacket the color of midnight. She paused in the doorway to admire the table.

"Nine plates? Optimist."

"An incurable condition, Miss Gordon. My doctors have given up."

"You might want to move the water glass at Jason's place. The last time he was here, he broke one during an argument about salad."

"I remember. I also remember that Master Jason was correct."

Dick laughed. "He was arguing that lettuce is a conspiracy."

"A defensible position when one has survived the produce available in Gotham."

Barbara kissed Alfred's cheek, then looked toward the staircase.

"Is he home?"

Alfred did not ask whom she meant.

"He was here this afternoon."

He surrendered. Stephanie slid the tablet into a drawer and sat down, victorious.

Cassandra Cain appeared behind her without sound, touched Stephanie's shoulder, and accepted a small wrapped chocolate from her hand. It was a transaction they had apparently negotiated long before either reached the dining room.

Damian Wayne arrived last among the younger members of the household, with a severe expression and a formal jacket he insisted was not formal.

He inspected the seating arrangement.

"Why am I beside Grayson?"

"Because," Alfred said, "the alternative was seating you beside Master Jason."

"Grayson is acceptable."

"I'm touched," Dick said.

"You shouldn't be."

"There he is."

Stephanie told a story about a man who tried to rob a bakery while wearing a replica of Batman's mask and surrendered when the owner threatened to call Robin. Tim argued that this was a statistically reasonable response. Damian objected to the implication that the title Robin was frightening in itself. Barbara accused Dick of stealing her favorite bicycle from the cave when they were teenagers. Dick claimed the bicycle had been abandoned. Cassandra reached across the table and tilted Dick's water glass back upright before his elbow hit it.

"Yes."

No one spoke.

Alfred put the phone away.

His eyes found the empty seat.

"Let me guess. Emergency."

"The Narrows," Tim said.

"Oh, good. At least it's geographically creative."

Alfred took Jason's coat before he could object.

"There's food in the kitchen."

Jason followed him.

Forty-one miles of Gotham streets away, Batman crouched on a narrow maintenance balcony overlooking an abandoned office building in the Narrows.

"Does it? How perceptive."

Bruce knew what that meant.

"Dinner ended twenty minutes ago."

"Alfred."

"Yes, sir?"

"Someone wanted me here."

"I suspect so."

"The call was false."

Alfred's voice changed. "You believe it was deliberate?"

"Yes."

Bruce waited for the rest.

"The other danger," Alfred said, "is still waiting at home."

The connection ended.

Batman remained on the balcony while the rain worked its way beneath his collar. Below him, Gotham kept moving. Cars crossed intersections. A diner glowed blue behind steamed windows. A father hurried a child across the street with his coat held over both their heads.

Bruce pressed his fist against the railing until the metal creaked.

There were no instructions for getting a wasted evening back.

There were no grapnel lines for it, either.

The Perfect Response

The first bank robbery began with a puppet making a speech.

People Who Keep Receipts

Barbara Gordon kept a clock in her office that ran five minutes fast.

She had done it deliberately. Every other device in the room synchronized to a time source with extraordinary precision, but the clock on the wall was a stubborn, mechanical reminder that an instrument was only as honest as the assumptions of the person reading it.

Her father hated it.

"Your clock's wrong," Commissioner Gordon said as he entered.

"Your tie's crooked."

He adjusted the tie, then stopped. "That was mean."

"You walked into my apartment and started insulting the furniture."

The apartment occupied the upper floors of a converted Gotham clocktower. Gordon folded his arms.

Arnold Wesker had once learned to repair watches.

His father had taught him with a cracked magnifying glass and a box of abandoned movements. A watch, his father said, was a collection of tiny parts that made an agreement to move together. Scarface's eyes seemed to narrow.

Arnold felt the puppet's jaw go still. It was a dangerous quiet.

"Home?" Scarface snapped. "You got a place with a leaking ceiling and somebody else's old furniture. You call that a home?"

The Family Portrait

Union Terminal stood on the east side of the Gotham River, a cathedral built for trains. Its great glass roof had survived a century of storms but not the decades of neglect that followed. Restoration crews had polished the brass railings and cleaned the enormous clock above the concourse. The hands still pointed to eleven seventeen, the time the station had closed for good.

That evening the clock was moving again.

Below it, a crowd had gathered to watch the old station's first illumination ceremony. Families held paper lanterns. Children wore cheap superhero masks. The city had invited everyone to celebrate its survival, an unusual Gotham tradition that generally lasted until somebody robbed something.

"You don't like nothing."

"Ladies and gentlemen, please remain calm."

"End this," Batman said.

"End what? I ain't started yet."

"He's using a public model," she said over the family channel. "People can see the predictions."

"Then let's disappoint him," Dick answered.

"Hey. Nice outfit. A little gloomy, but I respect the commitment."

The child pointed at him. "You're Nightwing!"

"Last time I checked. You mind helping me get everybody toward the staff entrance? Very important job."

The boy nodded solemnly and took his mother's hand.

"Damn," Dick muttered. "They're predicting the jokes now."

One of the screens flashed: LOW CONFIDENCE.

"That's encouraging," Tim said.

"I am powered entirely by bad decisions and snacks," Stephanie replied.

"Which explains a lot," Damian said.

He dropped from the upper gallery with the precise confidence of a young man who had never considered modesty a tactical advantage. Two of Scarface's men moved to intercept him. "Good work!"

"I did not ask for praise!"

"You're welcome!"

The woman was bleeding from a cut on her forehead. Damian guided her into cover before returning to the fight.

"I am always nice," Damian snapped.

"Damian," three voices replied together.

"Wesker," Batman called. "You don't have to do this."

Without speaking, she pointed at the empty space beside him. There was a way out. She wanted him to know it existed.

THANK YOU FOR THE REHEARSAL.

The lights came back.

"You saw the files?" Bruce asked.

"I know."

"The thing is," Dick said, "we were good tonight. Even when we weren't following your plan."

CHAPTER EIGHT
The File Cabinet

The HOMEGROUND archive occupied a single locked cabinet on the south side of the Batcave.

That was its physical form, anyway. The real archive had spread through years of backups, hardware changes, obsolete storage systems, and one deeply misguided project Bruce had once imagined would protect the people he loved. The cabinet held the paper originals, because he had never trusted a computer to remember something forever.

Dick opened it without asking.

Inside were narrow gray folders labeled with dates and case numbers. No names. The names were printed on the contents, a distinction that had once seemed professional. He took the first folder and found a diagram of his own movements on a rooftop when he was fourteen.

Barbara stood beside him.

"You don't have to read it," she said.

"I know."

He turned a page.

FEAR RESPONSE OBSERVED. SUBJECT MAINTAINED FUNCTION DESPITE INCREASED RESPIRATION. CONTINUE EXPOSURE.

Dick laughed once, a bitter, surprised sound.

"God, he really did think he was building something safer."

Barbara took a folder from farther back. She recognized the night immediately: a warehouse fire, a missing child, and a choice she had made to ignore Bruce's instruction because the fire would have reached the rear staircase before the rescue crew arrived. She had been right. The child had lived.

Her file described the decision as OPERATOR DISOBEDIENCE: ACCEPTABLE OUTCOME; INCREASE OVERSIGHT.

"He wasn't angry I disobeyed," she said. "He was angry it worked."

Tim, sitting at the computer, turned in his chair.

"He thought he could improve outcomes by predicting exceptions."

"That's the story he told himself," Barbara said. "It's also exactly what Strange is telling Gotham."

Tim looked at the file in his lap. He had already found his own. The pages were so detailed that they seemed to belong to someone who had never stopped watching him. He felt a private surge of shame at how often he had wanted Bruce to notice his efforts and how little he had understood the difference between being noticed and being cataloged.

Cass moved past them to the cabinet. She opened the drawer marked with her earliest patrols, examined a photograph of herself standing beneath a streetlamp, and closed it again.

"You don't want to know what he wrote?" Tim asked.

"I know what he saw," she answered. "I don't know what he missed."

She walked to Bruce's workbench, where a small box contained assorted gifts people had given him. A hand-painted card from Damian. A photograph of Stephanie making a ridiculous face. A bent paperclip Dick had fashioned into a bat during a long hospital wait. Cass found her own gift among them: a little folded paper crane she had made after the first night she slept in the manor without waking afraid.

Bruce had kept it.

She turned the crane in her hands.

A man could love someone and still do a terrible job of showing it. She had known that all her life. Love was not a defense against the damage.

"He kept the good things," she said.

Dick looked up. "What?"

Cass held up the paper crane. "He kept the good things, too."

That made the room quieter than anger had.

Jason arrived carrying a pizza box, because Jason refused to enter a room where people were confronting childhood trauma without making at least one person furious.

"Who's hungry?"

"We're reading files about how Dad assessed our nervous systems," Stephanie answered.

"Cool. Pepperoni?"

He set the box down, took a slice, and opened his own folder. He skimmed two pages. Then he closed it.

"Not tonight," he said.

Dick watched him. "You okay?"

"No. Stop asking everybody that like you're the designated functioning adult."

"Fair."

Jason leaned against the cabinet.

"You know what bothers me? He thought the lesson after I died was to collect more information. As if there was a number he could find that would make it impossible to lose anybody again."

Barbara nodded. "Strange thinks the same thing. Only he's using the numbers to take control of a city."

"So we beat him," Jason said. "Then what?"

Nobody answered.

He looked toward the empty chair in front of the computer.

"If we beat the bad guy and then go back to pretending Bruce didn't do this, Strange wins a little anyway."

The thought settled among them.

Dick took the first photograph out of his folder. He laid it beside Cass's paper crane and Jason's pizza box. Strange could predict movement, Bruce had predicted fear, and both of them had somehow missed the simplest question.

What did these people want from one another when no one was in danger?

Dick thought of the little girl at the gym, trusting the mat provisionally. He imagined standing opposite Bruce at dinner and saying the words he had been holding for years.

"Then we don't go back," he said.

The Shape of the Question

Lucius Fox had attended enough disastrous meetings to know that the worst ones began with someone saying, "We all want the same thing."

Dr. Hugo Strange began his with precisely those words.

Strange smiled. "Less than a continuing dependency on people whose identities and decisions we cannot scrutinize."

The vice president spoke quickly. "Any archival material in our possession would be subject to contractual controls--"

"Then you should have no objection to showing me the retention logs," Lucius said.

Strange regarded him with mild interest.

"I understand your employer is a man who values secrecy."

"I value accurate records," Lucius answered. "So does he, when he remembers to be an adult."

A nervous laugh moved around the table.

Cass waited. She did not tell Arnold the puppet was unreal or make a joke about his illness. She had spent too long being reduced to a history of what had been done to her. She knew the difference between telling someone what they were and giving them room to speak.

"Strange uses you," she said.

Arnold swallowed.

"Everybody uses somebody."

"Not everybody."

"He thinks he understands us. Every conversation, he watches. He writes down what makes me upset. Then he tells me what I'll do before I even know."

Arnold looked up. "Yes."

Scarface leaned forward. "I ain't small."

"You are," Cass said, looking straight at the puppet. "But loud."

The puppet went still.

Arnold made a tiny sound. It might have been a laugh.

"You think you're funny, huh?" Scarface demanded.

Cass shook her head. "Sometimes."

A silence passed. Outside, a bakery truck reversed with a long, apologetic beep. Arnold looked toward the clock. He reached behind the counter, took out a screwdriver, and opened the glass front.

"My father showed me how to make it run," he said. "You can fix some things. Other things, you have to admit they're finished."

"Tell me about Strange," Cass said.

Arnold turned a tiny brass mechanism in his hands. "He wants to show Gotham how he can predict everybody. Tomorrow night's ceremony. He said the whole city will be watching when the Bat has to choose between doing what the doctor expects and doing what his family needs."

"How?"

"I don't know. His people run the screens. He said there'd be a special demonstration at eleven seventeen. Like the old clock at the station."

Cass remembered the hands stopping during the rehearsal.

"Why eleven seventeen?"

Arnold's fingers tightened around the little mechanism.

"I asked him. He said it was the exact minute Batman failed to save somebody, many years ago. It was in one of the files. He said grief makes a good metronome because people keep returning to it."

"He'll hurt people," she said.

"He promised not to."

"Did you believe him?"

Arnold stared at the clock. A minute passed before he answered.

"I wanted to."

Scarface banged his wooden fist on the counter.

"What's with the interrogation? You a cop?"

"No," Cass answered.

"Then quit talking like one."

She looked at Arnold. "You can tell police. They can protect people. You will have to answer for what you did."

He flinched at the last sentence, but she did not soften it. She was not promising him escape from consequences. She was offering a choice he could make while consequences remained real.

"He has my records," Arnold said. "Private things. Things I told doctors when I thought nobody else would hear."

"That was wrong."

Arnold's eyes filled.

"He said it would make me better. Then he used it to make me afraid."

Cass reached into her pocket and placed a tiny paper crane on the counter. She had folded it from a receipt while walking through Gotham.

"This is yours," she said.

Arnold looked at the crane. "Why?"

"A choice. Keep it. Throw it away. I won't watch."

She stood and walked toward the door.

"Wait," Arnold said.

She turned.

"You didn't ask me to help you catch him."

"You know how to find me."

Scarface shook his little cigar angrily.

"Don't think we're gonna be your stool pigeons!"

Cass looked at him. "Wouldn't dream of it."

Arnold smiled, which changed his face more than Cass expected.

After she left he sat in the quiet shop for nearly an hour. He put the little crane beside the broken clock. Then he reached toward the gears and began working on the mechanism that had stopped.

"What are you doing?" Scarface asked.

"Fixing something."

"We got work tonight."

"I know."

"Don't go getting ideas."

Arnold placed the spring inside its housing. He turned the clock's minute hand to the correct time and listened as the pendulum resumed its small, stubborn journey.

"It's my shop," he said.

Scarface had no answer ready for that.

CHAPTER TWELVE
The Worst Man in the Room

Hugo Strange disliked being called a villain.

He had tried to explain this to several people over the years, some of them in offices, some on hospital wards, some while they were being escorted out by men who had been told not to listen. A villain pursued selfish ends. He pursued knowledge. If certain people suffered while contributing to knowledge, that was tragic, but it did not make the project evil.

The distinction pleased him. It allowed him to be curious about cruelty without feeling responsible for it.

He stood before a glass wall displaying a city in miniature. Gotham's bridges, tunnels, and neighborhoods glowed in a hundred colors, each represented by a predictive model that drew on public records, private files, and a distressing amount of material whose owners had never agreed to provide it.

His associate, a narrow man named Merrick Crain, approached with a report.

"Civic Horizon's board approved the demonstration. The council hasn't formally voted on procurement."

"They will," Strange said.

"The police are asking questions about Union Terminal."

"They should. Suspicion is a sign of active citizenship."

"They may cancel the event."

"Then the public will see its safety taken away by frightened men who cannot explain what they fear. I shall offer them a safer alternative."

Crain looked troubled. He was not a bad man in the operatic sense. He had accepted a job building software that promised to reduce injuries. Over time, the project had become a machine for turning other people's privacy into a product. He had never found the exact day on which he should have resigned.

"Dr. Strange," he said, "some of the data came from private medical interviews."

"Yes."

"And minors."

"Young people are often more candid about fear."

"That's not the point."

Strange turned.

"Then tell me the point, Mr. Crain."

Crain hesitated, and his hesitation found a place in Strange's mental catalog. Cowardice, Strange thought. A need to have principles only after the benefits of surrendering them had been collected.

"The point is that those people didn't agree," Crain said.

"Agreement is frequently obtained from people who cannot comprehend what they have agreed to. Would you prefer that fiction?"

"I'd prefer we stop."

Strange was silent for a moment. Then he smiled with genuine sadness.

"You have become inconvenient," he said.

Crain felt suddenly cold.

"You're firing me?"

"I'm relieving you of a burden. You were never suited to the difficult parts of this work."

Crain left. Strange had expected him to leave. He had also expected him to tell someone. It was one of the great comforts of predictive systems: betrayal could become merely another branch of the plan.

On the glass wall a pale dot marked Bruce Wayne's location at the manor. Surrounding it were seven smaller dots corresponding to the people he called family. Strange did not need access to every secure device to know roughly where they were; he had spent months assembling the ordinary traces people left in a city that could not stop observing them.

One of the dots was missing.

Arnold Wesker had departed his assigned location six hours earlier. His people had left a rented warehouse. The scheduled communications had ceased. Strange enlarged the map and frowned.

"An unfortunate deviation," he murmured.

He opened the file on Arnold, a devastating collection of interviews and clinical records. In the margins of one report a young physician had described a patient who apologized constantly and struggled to assert himself. Strange had marked the sentence: EXTERNAL AUTHORITY RESPONSE: HIGH.

Arnold should have obeyed.

Strange replayed the terminal incident. He watched the puppet swagger before the crowd and the man behind it tremble. He had understood the pair as a single mechanism, one part issuing orders and the other obeying. It had seemed so simple.

Yet Arnold had stepped away from the balcony when Cassandra Cain pointed out an exit. Not because of an order. Because a young woman had given him a choice.

Strange closed the file.

"Sentiment," he said, with the contempt of a man using an explanation where an understanding ought to be.

At the station, he planned to make sentiment measurable.

***

Bruce had been awake for twenty-six hours when Tim arrived with a folder marked INCIDENT ELEVEN SEVENTEEN.

"This is why he chose the time," Tim said.

Bruce opened it and saw a date from the worst week of his life. He recognized the minute before he recognized the event. Eleven seventeen. A call had gone unanswered. Someone he loved had needed him. The world had kept moving.

Jason.

Bruce shut the folder.

"He found it," he said.

"Yes."

Tim stood beside him in the cave. He had seen Batman stare down men with swords, guns, monsters, and impossible powers. He had not seen him look quite so small.

"He wants to force you to relive it in front of everyone," Tim said. "He's probably expecting you to withdraw from the plan."

Bruce looked toward Jason's old red helmet, standing behind glass.

"I should tell him."

"Jason already knows you keep the helmet."

"Not about this. About the time. The file. Why Strange chose it."

Tim nodded. "Then tell him."

Bruce placed the folder on the desk.

"He might not want to hear from me."

"You could ask."

Bruce glanced at him, and Tim let the look pass. The family was becoming intolerably consistent about this new method of problem-solving.

"I will," Bruce said.

Tim started toward the stairs, then stopped.

"There's something else. HOMEGROUND predicts that I'll try to keep everyone together because I'm afraid of another loss. Strange is going to expect me to coordinate."

"You are good at coordinating."

"I know. But maybe I should let somebody else do it."

Bruce looked at him carefully.

"What would you rather do?"

Tim smiled. "I have an idea that probably won't work."

"Tell me."

Tim told him.

Bruce listened without reaching for a correction.

CHAPTER THIRTEEN
What Gotham Knows

Commissioner Gordon had found that Gothamites tolerated a certain amount of absurdity provided it arrived with reliable public transportation.

They had endured costumed criminals, elaborate riddles, poison-laced parades, and several episodes in which a man with an umbrella had declared himself the rightful owner of the harbor. They complained about potholes with considerably more passion. The new Union Terminal was supposed to be the first good news in months, and the mayor wanted it opened before another scandal consumed the front page.

Gordon met with the mayor at half past ten.

"We have credible information that tonight's ceremony may be targeted," he said.

"Targeted how?"

"A man connected to last night's disruption is linked to the event's security contractor."

"We have extra police on the property."

"I'm asking you to consider postponement until we can verify the systems are safe."

The mayor studied him. "Jim, you know how much this costs. We've already postponed once."

"I also know how much a disaster costs."

"Do you have proof one is planned?"

"We have evidence a criminal intends to exploit the event. We don't have the whole mechanism yet."

"Then you do your job and keep people safe. I'll do mine and keep this city moving."

Gordon wanted to throw the mayor through the beautiful plate-glass window. Instead he returned to police headquarters and made certain every organizer had been briefed on the known risk. He asked the fire marshal for a fresh inspection and arranged direct lines to the station's staff. He notified hospitals and transport supervisors that public announcements from the venue should not be trusted without independent confirmation.

He did not pretend these measures would be enough. They were simply the things he had authority to do.

Barbara arrived at his office with two coffees.

"How'd it go?" she asked.

"About as well as a raccoon in a baptismal font."

She laughed. "Who taught you that?"

"Your mother."

Barbara sat across from him. "I found a link between Strange's trial presentation and the Wayne archive. Some of the code used to label partner responses came directly out of HOMEGROUND. Lucius has a written chain showing it was copied into a Civic Horizon migration vault and then used in the model."

"Good. That gives us grounds to seize records."

"It does. But I think he's going to release the information himself. He wants the city to see Batman isn't magical. He's just predictable."

Gordon took a drink of coffee.

"He'd be right about one thing. The man can be stubborn."

"He can. But it isn't the same thing as being incapable of change."

"You're speaking from experience?"

"Painful experience."

He regarded her with paternal concern that she had learned to endure without surrendering to it.

"You know you don't have to make this personal," he said.

"It's already personal. He used my private records. He used Dick's childhood. He found things about Jason nobody should have touched. And he thinks that makes him an expert on us."

"Then prove him wrong."

"Not by doing something random," she said. "That would just make us unpredictable in a stupid way. We need to make decisions based on what the people around us actually need, not what our old habits tell us to do."

Gordon smiled faintly. "You make that sound harder than it ought to be."

"It is harder. That's why people keep building systems to avoid it."

She finished the coffee and stood.

"I'm going to talk to the family."

"All of them?"

"Even Bruce."

Gordon raised an eyebrow.

"That's brave."

"Apparently it's a family trait."

***

On the east side of Gotham, a bus driver named Gloria Hernandez noticed that the station's practice announcements were telling passengers to enter by a closed gate. She called the transit supervisor and argued until he checked the schedule. The gate was opened by mistake in the simulation, a tiny detail that might have caused real trouble if nobody had bothered to notice.

At Gotham Memorial, an emergency nurse named Talia Brooks read the police advisory and asked her staff to make sure families waiting for discharged relatives knew which phone numbers were trustworthy. She had spent enough nights guiding worried people through bad information to know how quickly confusion multiplied.

A maintenance worker at Union Terminal saw an unfamiliar contractor's badge and called a supervisor rather than guessing that the stranger belonged there.

None of these people wore masks. None would make the evening news unless something went wrong. Their decisions were not dramatic. They were ordinary demonstrations of attention.

By afternoon, Barbara had collected eleven reports of small errors and irregularities. None of them alone proved what Strange intended. Together they suggested a pattern: the system was being adjusted to create a public impression that normal civic procedures were helpless without its predictions.

She showed the reports to Tim.

"Everybody's seeing pieces," he said.

"Exactly."

"So the family should be doing that too."

"That's the plan."

Tim looked surprised. "We have a plan?"

"We have a way to talk about one. That's different."

She passed him a stack of sandwiches from the station cafe.

"Feed Damian before he becomes a separate emergency."

"Good call."

As he left, Barbara thought of the little photograph that began it all: a boy on a beam, smiling because he was scared to let his father see the fear. The records captured the height, the fall risk, the pulse, and the moment of success. They did not capture the thing the boy had wanted most.

Somebody to catch him if he fell.

She wrote three words on the whiteboard above her desk.

ASK. LISTEN. TRUST.

Then, after a moment, she added a fourth.

VERIFY.

She was still Barbara Gordon, after all.

CHAPTER FOURTEEN
The Son Who Came Back

Jason Todd had four rules about Wayne Manor.

He did not stay overnight. He did not use the front entrance. He did not discuss his death as though it were an unfortunate school report. And he never, under any circumstances, allowed Bruce Wayne to make him tea.

At four in the afternoon, he broke the second rule and walked through the front door.

Bruce was standing in the library, looking at an old book he had not turned a page of in twenty minutes.

"You called," Jason said.

Bruce closed the book. "Thank you for coming."

"Let's not get sentimental. You said it was important."

"It is. Strange has a file from the night you died. The model uses that event as a reference point. Tomorrow, at eleven seventeen, he'll try to make me repeat the choices I made then."

Jason's face became very still.

"So the bastard's got a scrapbook."

"Yes."

"You knew it existed?"

"I recorded everything after I found out what happened. I kept going over the sequence. I thought if I understood the timing, I could prevent it from happening again."

Jason looked at the carpet. "And how's that been working out for you?"

Bruce accepted the question.

"Badly."

Jason laughed. It was an angry sound, but it was the first laugh either of them had heard in the room.

"Well, that's a start."

Bruce gestured toward a chair. Jason ignored it. He moved to the window and looked out at the grounds, at the place where he'd once learned to ride a motorcycle after Alfred declared it safer than having him practice on the highway.

"You know why I stopped coming here?" he asked.

Bruce waited.

"It wasn't because you didn't save me. I was furious about that, sure. I was furious about a hundred things. But people are allowed to fail. Even you."

He turned.

"I stopped coming because every time you looked at me, I could see the night I died reflected in your face. Like the person standing in front of you was less real than the person you couldn't get back."

Bruce's throat tightened.

"Jason--"

"You want me alive? Here I am. Alive. Angry. Sometimes an asshole. I make mistakes and I make choices you hate and sometimes you're right to hate them. But I'm not your lesson."

Bruce held his son's gaze.

"You're not."

"Then say who I am."

Bruce looked at the man before him. He saw the hard-won strength, the defiance, the fierce loyalty he expressed in ways that often made everything worse. He saw the child who had once stolen the wheels from a car that belonged to Batman and had laughed when he learned who the owner was. He saw the adult who had saved strangers more times than he would admit.

"You're Jason," he said. "My son. You're here."

Jason blinked and looked away.

"Yeah," he said quietly. "I am."

Bruce took one step closer, then stopped. He remembered what Barbara had told him in the kitchen.

"Would it be all right if I hugged you?" he asked.

Jason stared at him with such genuine astonishment that Bruce thought he might have said something ridiculous.

"Who the hell are you?" Jason demanded.

"I'm trying to do something differently."

"You want a medal?"

"No."

Jason looked back toward the window. His face worked for a moment. Then he crossed the room in three quick steps and threw his arms around Bruce so hard that the older man had to brace himself.

Bruce held him. He did not say he was sorry again. He did not explain the files. He did not try to make the past smaller. He just held the son who had come back, who was still here, who deserved to be known as more than a disaster survived.

After a while Jason pulled away.

"If you tell anybody I did that, I'm stealing the Batmobile."

Bruce's mouth twitched.

"You already have."

"And it was awesome."

They stood in the awkward, living quiet left behind after a difficult conversation.

"I'm not promising to do whatever you say tomorrow," Jason said.

"I'm not asking you to."

"And if Strange uses those files on me, I might get angry."

"You have a right to be."

"I might also make a really bad decision."

Bruce nodded. "Then I'll be there if you want help."

Jason took a breath.

"That's the thing," he said. "This time I think I might."

Alfred appeared at the door carrying a tray with two mugs.

Jason pointed at him. "Don't you dare."

"I assure you, Master Jason, the tea is entirely my doing. Master Bruce remains prohibited from operating the kettle without adult supervision."

Jason grinned in spite of himself.

Bruce looked at his son and made a small decision that Strange's files had never predicted.

He sat down and stayed.

CHAPTER FIFTEEN
No One in Charge

The most important Bat-family meeting in years took place in a diner because Barbara refused to attend another discussion in the Batcave.

"I am not arguing about autonomy while standing inside somebody else's giant underground bunker," she said.

Bruce accepted that, though not without a visible struggle. So at eight in the evening he entered a twenty-four-hour diner in the shadow of Gotham's old courthouse, removed his coat, and sat in a booth designed for people considerably smaller than him.

The booth made a noise like an old ship taking on water.

Stephanie looked up. "You're going to owe the diner a new table."

"The table is fine," Bruce said.

"It's praying."

Dick arrived last. He glanced at Bruce, exchanged a brief nod, and sat beside Barbara. They had not spoken privately since the archive was opened. Bruce could feel the distance between them as if it were a physical object on the table.

The waitress appeared, looked around at nine tired people in an assortment of expensive coats and clothes not designed for normal civilian life, and said, "Coffee?"

"God, yes," Tim said.

Alfred sighed. "For the love of all that is decent, Master Timothy, you need sleep."

"I had four hours."

"Over what interval?"

"That's invasive."

"Coffee," the waitress repeated.

"Bring a pot," Barbara said.

They ordered breakfast for dinner. Alfred called it a triumph of American civilization. Damian ordered a salad and looked personally betrayed when Stephanie added pancakes to the table for everyone.

Barbara spread a paper map of Union Terminal across the sticky surface between the syrup bottles.

"Strange expects a central commander," she said. "He expects Bruce to assign everyone a place. So we're not doing that. We'll identify the priorities, divide up responsibilities by agreement, and let the people closest to each problem make decisions."

Damian frowned. "A committee?"

"A family," Dick said.

"There's a difference?"

"We're usually worse dressed," Jason answered.

Barbara outlined the known facts. The public ceremony would begin at ten. The renovated terminal would remain open for guests, transit officials, and families. Civic Horizon planned to unveil its prediction software before the city council. Strange had arranged equipment and a live broadcast. His criminal associates had access to parts of the event's production organization, though the police were already scrutinizing that access.

"No one goes looking for a fight," she said. "The audience comes first. If something seems wrong, we tell the station staff and the police instead of trying to be clever by ourselves."

"That's a terrible superhero slogan," Stephanie said.

"It's an excellent public-safety slogan."

"Fine. I'll put it on a mug."

Tim laid out his discovery. "Strange's model updates itself when we use familiar methods. He gets better when we're chasing the thing he wants us to chase. So we need to stop treating the model like an opponent we can outsmart by being random. It won't matter if we just choose weird moves. He'll eventually learn those too."

"What do you propose?" Bruce asked.

Tim paused, astonished to be asked rather than corrected.

"We let the city's ordinary systems do their jobs," he said. "Gordon's people handle crowd safety. The station staff control exits. Lucius works through the legal audit. The family only does things we are uniquely equipped to do. And nobody makes decisions for the others."

"I like it," Dick said.

"It lacks a central point of failure," Barbara added.

"It's also less satisfying to an egomaniac," Jason observed.

They all looked at Bruce.

"I noticed," Bruce said.

The waitress came by with a coffeepot and a basket of toast. She glanced at the map.

"You all work for the city?"

"Family business," Alfred said.

She nodded with the weary comprehension of a woman who had spent her entire career hearing things she did not need to know.

"Good luck with that."

Once she left, Dick took a pen and drew a circle on the map around the main concourse.

"I'll handle evacuation coordination with the station workers, if they want me. Steph can help with the crowd."

"I'd rather work with people than screens," Stephanie said. "Done."

"I'll talk to Arnold," Cassandra said.

"I'll go with her," Jason offered. "If Scarface's boys get twitchy, I can keep them busy."

Barbara raised an eyebrow. "Without escalating?"

Jason placed a hand over his heart. "You wound me."

"Jason."

"Yes. Without escalating unless somebody's in danger."

Tim took responsibility for documenting any false predictions and sharing real-time changes with Barbara. Damian chose to stay close to the public first-aid stations, where he could protect people without needing to demonstrate his superiority over everyone older than him.

He objected when the others described this as his own idea.

"It is my idea," he said. "I simply object to your satisfaction about it."

Barbara looked toward Bruce.

"What do you want to do?"

He studied the map. There was a time when he would have announced where everyone belonged before anyone asked. The habit rose in him, strong and comforting.

Then he looked at the people around the table.

"I want to be where the help is needed," he said. "And I'd like somebody to tell me if I'm getting in the way."

Jason nearly dropped his fork.

"Someone check his pulse."

"His pulse is fine," Tim said. "I checked it."

Everyone stared at him.

"What? It's a public medical observation."

Cassandra laughed. Damian rolled his eyes. Barbara watched Bruce with a small expression that was not yet forgiveness but was no longer quite anger.

Bruce approached carefully.

"Thank you for coming," he said.

Dick nodded. "The pancakes were good."

"They were."

Bruce looked at the reflection of the diner lights in the window. "I know we need to talk."

"We do."

"Will you talk to me? After tomorrow?"

Dick studied him for a long moment. "If you're asking, yes. If you're scheduling a debrief, no."

Bruce nodded. "I'm asking."

Dick put on his coat.

"Then don't disappear when it's uncomfortable."

He left before Bruce could answer.

Alfred joined Bruce at the register and inspected the bill.

"Well, sir," he said, "we have managed dinner without a structural collapse."

"The booth survived."

CHAPTER SIXTEEN
Founders' Night

Gotham came to Union Terminal dressed as though a city could improve its luck by wearing better clothes.

The reopened station glowed beneath strings of warm lamps. Brass signs shone over restored ticket counters. A string quartet played beneath the great clock, and volunteers handed children miniature cardboard locomotives. The mayor arrived surrounded by cameras and a pair of security officers who looked disapprovingly at the crowd.

On the platform nearest the river, a little boy asked his grandmother whether Batman was coming.

"I hope he doesn't have to," she answered.

That, Bruce thought from a rooftop across the street, was the most sensible thing anybody had said all night.

He was armored and ready, but the Batmobile was parked several blocks away and his gauntlet displayed none of the ordinary command structure. Barbara had insisted on an information channel in which everyone could send reports, but nobody could silently issue orders to another person. Tim had christened it the Family Group Chat. Bruce had refused the name. The name had won.

His earpiece chimed.

STEPH: The mayor's speech is scheduled for ten twenty. I recommend everyone bring snacks.

DAMIAN: This is a professional channel.

JASON: You are twelve.

DAMIAN: I am not twelve.

DICK: Everybody behave. We have civilians in the area.

STEPH: Look who's suddenly the adult.

BRUCE: Report relevant activity only.

BARBARA: Bruce.

BRUCE: Understood.

He could hear Barbara smiling. It unnerved him.

Inside the station, Alfred occupied a quiet table near the catering area in a perfectly ordinary dark suit. He had declined to remain in the cave. He had informed Bruce that if the family was to behave as one, it might be helpful for the oldest member to be present rather than broadcasting from a bunker like a disembodied school principal.

Lucius stood beside the foundation trustees, speaking with a representative from the city's privacy office. He carried the documented evidence of the unauthorized records, copies already secured with independent counsel. The evidence would not disappear if anything happened to him. He had made that clear to the people who had tried to persuade him to stop asking questions.

Gordon's officers were on duty throughout the venue. The fire marshal had inspected the main approaches and was standing beside the station manager, a short woman named Grace Okafor who had restored more of the building than the mayor knew existed. She looked like someone who was already tired of the mayor's speech.

At ten nineteen, the event began.

The mayor thanked everyone for believing in Gotham. People clapped. The string quartet played an optimistic arrangement of a song about homecoming. On a large screen behind the podium, Dr. Hugo Strange's name appeared beneath a polished Civic Horizon logo.

Barbara watched from an upper gallery.

"There he is," she said.

Strange strode onto the stage with the relaxed smile of a man who believed everyone in the room had come for him.

"Gotham City," he began, "has never lacked courage. It has lacked the tools to make courage unnecessary."

A few people applauded. Barbara muttered, "Well, that's an alarming thesis."

Strange presented his system. It would anticipate risks, organize responses, and spare the city the uncertainty of relying on self-appointed guardians. He demonstrated predictions of crowd movements and emergency decisions using anonymized figures that Barbara knew were not anonymous at all.

Then he paused beneath the clock.

"Of course," he said, "no system can be judged by an uncomplicated evening."

The station lights dimmed.

A low warning tone sounded. The screens displayed a simulated danger indicator at the west entrance and directed guests toward the south concourse. People turned in confusion.

Gordon's voice came over the family channel. "The station manager says that message didn't come from her team. We're switching to verified staff announcements."

Dick was already speaking with the nearest ushers. "We'll guide folks where the staff want them. No stampede, no panic."

Barbara glanced at the displays. "It's starting."

On the stage Strange looked almost pleased by the reaction he had created.

"Observe," he told the cameras. "When ordinary people face uncertainty, they seek the shortest path to certainty. That is entirely human. That is why Gotham needs this technology."

He raised one hand. A graphic appeared on the screen predicting a tall black figure's entrance from the eastern balcony in six seconds.

The countdown began.

Six.

Five.

Four.

Batman did not move.

Three.

Two.

One.

Nothing happened.

The room hesitated. People looked toward the balcony. A few laughed uncertainly.

Strange's expression tightened. He had not expected Bruce to remain on the roof outside while others handled the situation.

"Interesting," he murmured.

Then came a voice that did not belong to any system Strange controlled.

"HEY, DOC! YOU FORGOT TO INVITE THE ENTERTAINMENT!"

A small striped figure appeared on the edge of the balcony above the stage.

Arnold Wesker stood behind him, clutching the railing. Three members of Scarface's gang occupied the side gallery. One held a sack that had once contained promotional gifts. Another was eating an expensive pastry. Their arrival was six minutes ahead of the schedule Strange had given them.

"You're early," Strange said through gritted teeth.
